steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Robotic systems are more and more deployed in safety-critical applications, for example search and rescue in hazardous environments. Usually safety requirements are formulated as positive invariance of some given regions in the state space. If safety is violated, this could cause catastrophic damage to robots, harm to humans that co-exist in the field of activities, and economic loss. Control barrier function (CBF)-based approaches are a popular class of methods for safety-critical synthesis. A CBF defines a positive invariant set inside the safety region, so that when the robot reaches the boundary of the set, the control input will steer the robot towards the interior of the set.

The choice of barrier functions strongly affects the performance and the safety guarantees of CBF-based approaches. There is increasing interest in neural control barrier functions (NCBFs), which represent CBFs using neural networks. Polynomial CBFs are found by sum-of-squares (SOS) optimization, but NCBFs use the universal approximation power of neural networks. This allows CBFs to be applied to high-dimensional complex systems, for example learning-enabled robotic systems and neural network dynamical models.

Gap:
- NCBFs developed for fault- and attack-free environments
- sensors on robots vulnerable to faults and malicious attacks
- our experiments: NCBF safety guarantees fail in adversarial environments

This paper:
- safety-critical control under sensor faults and attacks
- adversary picks one of finitely many fault/attack patterns (distinct subset of compromised sensors)
- FT-NCBFs + data-driven learning; quadratic program for control inputs
- robot moves toward interior of positive invariant set under all attack patterns -> safety if set inside safety region

Contributions:
- FT-NCBFs, necessary and sufficient conditions, data-driven learning
- fault-tolerant control framework, proof of safety under all patterns
- case studies: mobile robot obstacle avoidance, spacecraft rendezvous; baseline with existing NCBFs fails

Organization: Section II preliminaries/problem, III solution, IV safety guarantee, V conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Robotic systems are more and more deployed in safety-critical applications, for example search and rescue in hazardous environments. Usually safety requirements are formulated as positive invariance of some given regions in the state space. If safety is violated, this could cause catastrophic damage to robots, harm to humans that co-exist in the field of activities, and economic loss. Control barrier function (CBF)-based approaches are a popular class of methods for safety-critical synthesis. A CBF defines a positive invariant set inside the safety region, so that when the robot reaches the boundary of the set, the control input will steer the robot towards the interior of the set.

The choice of barrier functions strongly affects the performance and the safety guarantees of CBF-based approaches. There is increasing interest in neural control barrier functions (NCBFs), which represent CBFs using neural networks. Polynomial CBFs are found by sum-of-squares (SOS) optimization, but NCBFs use the universal approximation power of neural networks. This allows CBFs to be applied to high-dimensional complex systems, for example learning-enabled robotic systems and neural network dynamical models.

Right now, NCBFs are developed for robotic systems that are designed to operate in environments without faults and attacks. But the sensors mounted on robotic systems have been shown to be vulnerable to a wide range of faults and malicious attacks. Our experiments show that the safety guarantees of NCBFs do not hold when robots operate in such adversarial environments.

In this paper we study safety-critical control of robotic systems under sensor faults and attacks. We consider an adversary that can choose an arbitrary fault or attack pattern among finitely many choices, and each pattern corresponds to a distinct subset of compromised sensors. We propose a new class of CBFs that we call fault-tolerant NCBFs (FT-NCBFs), and we present a data-driven method to learn them. Then, given the learned FT-NCBFs, we formulate a quadratic program that computes control inputs. These control inputs guarantee that the robot moves towards the interior of the positive invariant set defined by the FT-NCBF under all attack patterns. So we can guarantee the robot's safety by making sure that the positive invariant set is contained in the safety region. Our contributions are as follows.

- We propose FT-NCBFs for robotic systems under sensor faults and attacks. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for FT-NCBFs to guarantee safety, and based on these conditions we develop a data-driven method for learning FT-NCBFs.

- We develop a fault-tolerant framework that uses the FT-NCBFs for safety-critical control synthesis. We prove that the control inputs it synthesizes guarantee safety under all fault and attack patterns.

- We evaluate the approach with two case studies, the obstacle avoidance problem of a mobile robot and the spacecraft rendezvous problem. Our approach guarantees that the robot satisfies the safety constraint no matter what the faults and attacks are, while the baseline that uses existing NCBFs fails.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II gives preliminaries and the problem formulation. Section III presents our solution and Section IV shows its safety guarantee. Section V concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Robotic systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications such as search and rescue in hazardous environments [1,2,3]. Safety requirements are normally formulated as the positive invariance of given regions in the state space. Violating safety could lead to catastrophic damage to robots, harm to humans that co-exist in the field of activities, and economic loss [4,5]. A popular class of methods for safety-critical synthesis is control barrier function (CBF)-based approaches [6,7,8,9]. A CBF defines a positive invariant set within the safety region such that, when the robot reaches the boundary of the set, the control input steers the robot towards the interior of the set.

The performance and safety guarantees of CBF-based approaches depend strongly on the choice of barrier functions. Neural control barrier functions (NCBFs) [10,11,12], which represent CBFs using neural networks, have attracted increasing interest. Compared with polynomial CBFs found by sum-of-squares (SOS) optimization [13,14,15,16,17], NCBFs leverage the universal approximation power of neural networks [18,19,20], and thus allow CBFs to be applied to high-dimensional complex systems [21,22,11,23,24,25], e.g., learning-enabled robotic systems [26] and neural network dynamical models [27,28].

At present, NCBFs [10,11,12,29,30,31] are developed for robotic systems designed to operate in fault- and attack-free environments. However, sensors mounted on robotic systems have been shown to be vulnerable to a wide range of faults and malicious attacks [32,33]. As our experiments demonstrate, the safety guarantees of NCBFs do not hold when robots operate in such adversarial environments.

In this paper, we study the problem of safety-critical control of robotic systems under sensor faults and attacks. We consider an adversary that can choose an arbitrary fault or attack pattern among finitely many choices, where each pattern corresponds to a distinct subset of compromised sensors. We propose a new class of CBFs called fault-tolerant NCBFs (FT-NCBFs) and present a data-driven method to learn them. Given the learned FT-NCBFs, we then formulate a quadratic program to compute control inputs. The resulting control inputs guarantee that the robot moves towards the interior of the positive invariant set defined by the FT-NCBF under all attack patterns. Consequently, we can guarantee the robot's safety by ensuring that the positive invariant set is contained within the safety region. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions.

- We propose FT-NCBFs for robotic systems under sensor faults and attacks. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for FT-NCBFs to guarantee safety, and based on these conditions we develop a data-driven method to learn FT-NCBFs.

- We develop a fault-tolerant framework that utilizes the proposed FT-NCBFs for safety-critical control synthesis. We prove that the synthesized control inputs guarantee safety under all fault and attack patterns.

- We evaluate our approach using two case studies: the obstacle avoidance problem of a mobile robot and the spacecraft rendezvous problem. We show that our approach guarantees that the robot satisfies the safety constraint regardless of the faults and attacks, whereas the baseline employing existing NCBFs fails.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents preliminaries and the problem formulation. We present our solution in Section III and demonstrate its safety guarantee in Section IV. Section V concludes the paper.
